title: Alzheimer and depressive cognitive-like behaviors in male and female rats: A new method for exposure to ambient air pollution
author: Motesaddi Zarandi, Shahsavani, et al.
materials: One-fourth of each QM filter was shredded into 15 mL Teflon container. Then, 2.5 mL CH₃OH and 2.5 mL of CH₂Cl₂ were added in Teflon container and was sonicated in an ultrasonic bath with 20 kHz for 30 min (Elmasonic S 80H). Finally, solutions were filtered via 0.22 μm Millipore PTFE filters (Hesperia, CA, USA). The concentration of 16-PAHs was performed using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) (Agilent model 5890A). Operating parameters of GC–MS presented was demonstrated in Table 2s.

steps.title: Prepare PM2.5 + gas chamber
steps.instruction: Connect urban ambient air at 12 L/min to exposure chamber 1 using an Echo PM (TCR Tecora, Italy) low‑volume sampler (LVS) with the sampling filter removed and a PM2.5 warhead installed, so outlet air contains ambient PM2.5 plus gaseous pollutants.

steps.title: Prepare gas‑only chamber
steps.instruction: Connect urban ambient air at 12 L/min to exposure chamber 2 via a vacuum pump (Model LFS‑113; Gillian Instrument Corp.) equipped with a HEPA filter model H13 (Camfill‑FARR, Switzerland) placed in the inlet valve to remove particles (≥99.97% efficiency); outlet air therefore contains gaseous pollutants only.

steps.title: Prepare clean‑air control chamber
steps.instruction: Supply ambient air at 12 L/min to the control chamber using a vacuum pump fitted with a HEPA filter model H13 (SungJin Co., Ltd., Korea) in the inlet valve and an active‑carbon air filter in the outlet valve, thereby removing both particulate and gaseous pollutants.

steps.title: Digest filters for metal analysis
steps.instruction: Process one‑fourth of each quartz‑membrane (QM) filter as follows:

substeps.instruction: Shred the portion into a 15 mL Teflon digestion vessel.
Add 2.5 mL concentrated HNO₃ (69 %) and 2.5 mL concentrated HClO₄ (70 %).
Heat at 170 °C for 4 h until the mixture dries.
Place the dried residue on a hot plate and dry further at 95–100 °C.
Add 2.5 mL HNO₃ and 2.5 mL distilled water, then shake at 180 rpm for 30 min.
Filter the solution through Whatman filter paper No 42 (125 mm).
Dilute the filtrate to a final volume of 10 mL and store in a plastic vial at 4 °C until ICP‑MS analysis.
Prepare a blank sample by digesting a clean Whatman filter alongside the test samples.

steps.title: Digest filters for PAH analysis
steps.instruction: Process one‑fourth of each QM filter as follows:

substeps.instruction: Shred the portion into a 15 mL Teflon digestion vessel.
Add 2.5 mL methanol (CH₃OH) and 2.5 mL dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂).
Sonicate in an ultrasonic bath (20 kHz) for 30 min using an Elmasonic S 80H device.
Filter the extract through a 0.22 µm Millipore PTFE filter.

steps.title: Analyze metals by ICP‑MS
steps.instruction: Inject the diluted metal digests into an ICP‑MS (Model 7900, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) and quantify metals using the instrument parameters described in Table 1s.

steps.title: Analyze PAHs by GC‑MS
steps.instruction: Inject the filtered PAH extracts into a GC‑MS (Agilent model 5890A) and quantify the 16 target PAHs using the instrument parameters described in Table 2s.

description: Air pollution is a complex mixture of gases, particulate matter (PM), metals and organic compounds [1]. Recently global concerns increased due to the adverse effects of air pollution on human health [2]. In this regard, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) declared that air pollution is definitive carcinogenic (Group 1) for humans [3]. The relationship between the exposure to air pollution and autoimmune diseases [4], cardiovascular diseases [5], asthma [6], chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) [7], and cognitive disorders [8] were well approved. PM classified as the ultrafine (≤0.1 μm), fine (≤2.5 μm) and coarse (2.5–10 μm), and particles [9]. Due to disperse uniformly, remaining as suspended in the air for a long period time, capability of penetration into the deepest respiratory system exposure to PM2.5 is a matter of concern [10]. Also, due to the high surface area of PM2.5, it can bind with metals, heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), metalloids, elemental carbon, organic carbon, ammonium, sulfate, nitrate, viruses, bacteria, which could increase adverse health effects [11]. Approximately 7.6% (42 million) of the total number of deaths worldwide is related to Exposure to PM2.5 [12]. PAHs in the air and bound PM2.5 have mutagenic and/or carcinogenic properties [13] and the metals include chromium (Cr), lead (Pb), arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), nickel (Ni), manganese (Mn) and copper (Cu) bound with PM2.5 induced to oxidative stress [14], following with an increase in DNA lesions [15]. The association between air pollution and neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative as one of the routes for increasing neurodegenerative disorders (ND) was approved [16,17]. However, pathophysiological mechanisms on the central nervous system (CNS) due to PM exposure is elucidated [18].
